posts.topic: YC-backed AI startup offered job interviews for company tattoos, then apologized
posts.script:

topic.title: OpenAI's Astra Solves 10 Decades-Old Math Problems for $2,000
topic.why: OpenAI's unreleased Astra model formally settled ten long-standing open problems in math and theoretical computer science, with full proof certificates, for about $2,000 in compute -- a preview of the reasoning power headed for every knowledge worker's toolkit.

posts.script:
OpenAI's next model just did something wild -- solved ten math problems nobody's cracked in over a decade, and it cost about two thousand dollars.

Astra, still unreleased, produced an explicit construction of a non-sofic group -- a question open since 1999 -- disproved Connes's rigidity conjecture on von Neumann algebras, and resolved three problems from Paul Erdos's famous list. OpenAI published a 249-page manuscript with machine-checked Lean 4 proof certificates on GitHub, and the verification count came back at zero errors. Total compute bill: roughly $2,000 at GPT-5.6 Sol API rates.

If reasoning this deep gets this cheap, every knowledge worker's toolkit is about to get a serious upgrade.

posts.topic: Anthropic starts watermarking all of Claude's output worldwide under new EU AI Act rules
posts.script:
Anthropic just started invisibly watermarking every piece of Claude's text and file output -- worldwide. It's compliance with the EU AI Act's Article 50, which took effect August 2nd and requires AI systems to mark synthetic content as machine-generated. The watermark is imperceptible to readers but detectable by tools built to spot it, and non-compliance can cost providers up to €15 million or 3% of global revenue. Anthropic joins roughly 190 signatories who backed the EU's Code of Practice on AI transparency this July. It's a preview of the disclosure standards every knowledge worker using AI tools will soon have to live with, whichever model they pick.

posts.topic: 90% of execs say 3 years of AI hasn't moved headcount or output
posts.script:
Three years into the AI boom, ninety percent of executives say it still hasn't moved their bottom line.

A new NBER survey of nearly six thousand CEOs and CFOs across the US, UK, Germany, and Australia found about ninety percent see zero measurable impact from AI on productivity or employment over that span. Here's the twist: nearly seventy percent of those same executives use AI less than an hour a week themselves -- twenty-eight percent never touch it at all. Yet companies keep citing AI in layoffs anyway; Deutsche Bank analysts call it "AI redundancy washing."

So if AI panic has you worried about your job, the data says most companies haven't even figured out how to use it themselves yet.
